beats.caption: RF chips sit between the antenna and the modem
beats.text: This GPU board has no radio: RF (radio-frequency) chips live in phones, base stations, Wi-Fi gear and satellites. Beside the board is a phone's RF front-end module, the block between antenna and modem, drawn large with its shield lifted off.

beats.caption: Inside: amplifiers, a switch and a row of filters
beats.text: On a small laminate sit a power amplifier (PA, often gallium arsenide) to transmit, a low-noise amplifier (LNA) to receive, an antenna switch to pick the band, and acoustic filters (BAW/SAW) that pass only one band each. A 5G phone needs dozens of bands, so it carries many filters.

beats.caption: Transmit: the PA boosts the signal out through a filter
beats.text: The transceiver's weak signal enters the PA, leaves a few hundred milliwatts strong, passes the band's filter so it does not spill into neighbours, then the switch routes it to the antenna, which radiates it.

beats.caption: Receive: a faint signal, cleaned and amplified
beats.text: Incoming signals can be a billionth of a milliwatt. The switch sends them through the right filter to the LNA, which lifts them while adding as little noise as possible before the transceiver digitizes them.

beats.caption: A BAW filter: a vibrating sliver of crystal
beats.text: Each filter is built from bulk acoustic wave (BAW) resonators: a thin piezoelectric film (aluminium nitride) between metal electrodes, over a mirror stack. It rings mechanically at one GHz frequency, so only that band passes. Revenue tracks handset cycles and band counts. Makers: Qorvo (QRVO), Skyworks (SWKS), Broadcom (AVGO), Qualcomm (QCOM), Murata.
